top_choice_rationale: P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is a bounded, mature discovery: it solved the problem of recovering substitution patterns and markups when prices are endogenous and products are differentiated. The credit traces to Berry (1994) and Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995). Roughly thirty years of use in merger review, regulation, auctions, trade and health, checked against outcomes such as merger retrospectives, support its maturity. The citation is limited to demand and competition estimation, which keeps attribution defensible. The omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin is a real cost of the three-name cap, but it is acceptable under a narrow citation. I rank P001 (Kiyotaki-Moore) second because it has an equally clean originating pair and wider conceptual reach, and the 2022 adjacency should count for little. I weigh B047's more settled applied record slightly higher. The margin is narrow and rests on weighting, not on a decisive scientific difference. P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is third because the local-labour-market effects and shift-share inference are still debated, and some overlap with earlier prizes remains. Any of the three is preferable to no award. This assessment rests on background knowledge, not verified citation data.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile for P001, P002 or P003 and their credited names. I am a Stockholm University colleague, in a different department, of Hassler, Krusell and Boppart, who support or have stated views on the proposals. The B021 political-economy ballot, where my profile shows a tie to Persson and Rothstein, is not on the slate. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
